items.sourceNote: For a few weeks around July, rain becomes the default state and umbrellas become clothing. 장마 has start dates, forecasts, and its own mood. Alongside 미세먼지 season and 벚꽃 season, it's proof Korea runs on many more than four seasons.

target.literal_gap: Literally “the road is blocked”; in use, “traffic is bad”.

items.sourceNote: No word for 'traffic jam' needed — the road itself gets stopped up, like a pipe. The same verb clogs noses (코가 막혀요) and speechless moments (말이 막혀요). One metaphor, many blockages.

target.literal_gap: Literally “engineer-sir”; in use, “how you address any driver”.

items.sourceNote: Korean rarely uses names with strangers — jobs + 님 do the work: 기사님 (driver), 사장님 (owner), 선생님 (teacher, or any respectable stranger). Address people by their role worn with honor, and doors open. Literally, sometimes.

target.literal_gap: Literally “the last vehicle”; in use, “the night's true deadline”.

items.sourceNote: Seoul's subway sleeps around midnight, so 막차 시간 quietly governs every evening's social physics — the glance at the phone, the 먼저 가요, the sprint through the station. Miss it and the night gets a taxi-fare surcharge.

target.literal_gap: Literally “house-entering”; in use, “housewarming party”.

items.sourceNote: Move into a new place and you owe your people a 집들이. Guests traditionally bring 휴지 (toilet paper) or 세제 (detergent) — long rolls and rising bubbles mean a long life and growing fortune. The host cooks; the guests admire the view; everyone asks about the rent.

target.literal_gap: Literally “warm stone”; in use, “Korean underfloor heating”.

items.sourceNote: Traditionally, kitchen smoke was routed under stone floors; today hot-water pipes do the job in every apartment. It's why floors are for sitting and sleeping, why an 이불 on the 바닥 beats a cold bed, and why shoes stop at the 현관 — you don't wear the street across a surface you sleep on.

items.english: I'm exhausted / so done with today

target.natural_english: I'm exhausted / so done with today
target.literal_gap: Literally “I want to go home”; in use, “I'm exhausted / so done with today”.

items.sourceNote: Said at desks, in classrooms, in queues — and, famously, while already at home. When there's no energy left for anything, the stated destination is 집, even if you're sitting in it. M3's -고 싶어요 doing emotional heavy-lifting.

target.literal_gap: Literally “body-ache”; in use, “the flattened-by-overwork illness”.

items.sourceNote: Not quite flu, not quite fatigue: the full-body collapse Korean recognizes as its own named disease — 몸살이 났어요, and everyone nods. Doctors prescribe 푹 쉬세요; grandmothers prescribe soup. That the language needs this word says something about the work culture.

target.literal_gap: Literally “I'm hungry to death”; in use, “I'm SO hungry”.

items.sourceNote: Korean hyperbole's favorite engine: [feeling] + 죽겠어요 = dying of it. 더워 죽겠어요 (dying of heat), 힘들어 죽겠어요 (dying of hardship). Nobody is dying; everybody says it hourly. English does 'starving to death' — Korean industrialized the pattern.

target.literal_gap: Literally “one's hands are big”; in use, “generous (always over-caters)”.

items.sourceNote: Said of the host who cooks for twelve when four are coming. The body is Korean's favorite metaphor kit: 코가 높다 (high nose — arrogant), 입이 무겁다 (heavy mouth — keeps secrets), 귀가 얇다 (thin ears — easily swayed). Glove size is not the point.

target.literal_gap: Literally “to see an exam”; in use, “to take an exam”.

items.sourceNote: Korean doesn't take tests — it SEES them. 시험을 봐요 (I'm taking a test), 시험을 잘 봤어요 (it went well). English 'sits' exams in Britain and 'takes' them in America; Korean watches them happen. Same verb as seeing a movie.

items.english: the exam that stops the nation

target.natural_english: the exam that stops the nation
target.literal_gap: Literally “scholastic ability (exam)”; in use, “the exam that stops the nation”.

items.sourceNote: One November morning, all of Korea holds its breath: flights are grounded during the listening section, offices open late to clear the roads, police escort late students with sirens on, and juniors cheer at the school gates. Twelve years of 학원 evenings aim at this single day.

target.literal_gap: Literally “Mon-Tue-Wed-Thu-Fri-Fri-Fri”; in use, “the week with no weekend”.

items.sourceNote: Take M5's weekday names, delete the weekend, photocopy Friday over it: the seven-day workweek as dark comedy. Office workers say it the way soldiers sing marching songs. Its existence — like 몸살's — is a cultural x-ray.

target.literal_gap: Literally “big gourd”; in use, “awesome! / no way! / jackpot”.

items.sourceNote: From folktale gourds that split open full of treasure. Now the all-purpose amazement word — a goal, a plot twist, a friend's news, a good 치킨 place. Positive or scandalized depending entirely on the eyebrows.

target.literal_gap: Literally “have you had your meal?”; in use, “hello / how are you”.

items.sourceNote: A greeting, not a lunch offer — from eras when the answer wasn't guaranteed to be yes. 밥 먹었어요? is its casual twin. Answer 네 and move on; nobody is feeding anybody. Caring about someone's meals IS caring about them — the whole culture in one question.

target.literal_gap: Literally “alone-rice”; in use, “eating alone (as a named act)”.

items.sourceNote: 혼자 + 밥, compressed. That Korean NEEDED this word says everything: meals were so default-communal that solo dining required naming. The family grows — 혼술 (drinking alone), 혼영 (movies alone) — as the culture makes peace with company-of-one.

target.literal_gap: Literally “(maternal) aunt!”; in use, “excuse me! (to a restaurant auntie)”.

items.sourceNote: In casual restaurants, the middle-aged server is summoned as family — 이모, mom's-side aunt, the warmest title available. It buys better 반찬 refills than 저기요 ever will. Use only where aprons and floor seating suggest it; the 부장님's French place, not so much.

items.english: friend; also 'fellow' for a peer or younger person

target.natural_english: friend; also 'fellow' for a peer or younger person
target.literal_gap: Literally “friend”; in use, “friend; also 'fellow' for a peer or younger person”.

items.sourceNote: As an ordinary noun, 친구 means a close friend; that friend can be older or younger than you. In a separate familiar or sometimes impolite use, 이 친구 can mean 'this fellow' when referring to someone around your age or younger. Age may affect how you address someone, but it does not decide whether that person is your 친구.

items.english: to be in the flirty maybe-stage

target.natural_english: to be in the flirty maybe-stage
target.literal_gap: Literally “to ride a something”; in use, “to be in the flirty maybe-stage”.

items.sourceNote: From English 'something' — as in, there's SOMETHING between them. The named stage before 사귀다: texting too often, denying it to friends. 썸 타는 중이야 — I'm riding a something. English needed this word and never made it; Korean borrowed the raw material and built it.

target.literal_gap: Literally “Ka-Talk (KakaoTalk)”; in use, “Korea's messaging operating system”.

items.sourceNote: Not an app — infrastructure. Work, family, 회식 planning, wedding invites, paying friends back: all 카톡. 카톡해! replaced 전화해! for a generation, and 단톡방 — the group chat — is where Korean social life actually lives. The yellow icon is on every phone in the country; opting out is a lifestyle statement.

target.literal_gap: Literally “read-and-chewed”; in use, “left on read”.

items.sourceNote: 읽다 (read) + 씹다 (to chew — slang for ignoring): they READ your message and said nothing. The 1 next to your 카톡 message disappears when read — so 읽씹 is provable, timestamped, and litigated between friends accordingly. English got 'left on read' years later; Korea had already compressed it to two syllables.

target.literal_gap: Literally “certification shot”; in use, “the proof photo”.

items.sourceNote: 인증 (verification) + 샷 (shot): the photo that PROVES it — you ran, you voted, you found the 맛집, you actually met. Korean internet culture treats experiences as claims requiring evidence; the 인증샷 is the receipt. It's why the 셀카 arm extends before the food gets touched.

target.literal_gap: Literally “clothes are wings”; in use, “clothes make the person”.

items.sourceNote: The proverb behind every makeover scene: dress someone well and they fly. Where English clothes 'make the man,' Korean gives them wings — same wisdom, better aerodynamics. Quoted whenever someone shows up unexpectedly well-dressed.

items.english: luxury brands (and the culture around them)

target.natural_english: luxury brands (and the culture around them)
target.literal_gap: Literally “name-goods”; in use, “luxury brands (and the culture around them)”.

items.sourceNote: 명 (name — 별명's 명) + 품 (goods): goods with a NAME. Korea is a per-capita luxury heavyweight — department-store lines before opening, first-job bag rituals. The word carries the whole phenomenon: aspiration, gifting etiquette, and the gravitational pull of a logo.

target.literal_gap: Literally “couple look”; in use, “deliberately matching couple outfits”.

items.sourceNote: M19's 커플 + look: dressing identically ON PURPOSE — matching tees, jackets, down to 커플 신발. Peak commitment display at theme parks and Jeju. Western couples match by accident and apologize; Korean couples match by appointment and photograph it (인증샷, naturally).

target.literal_gap: Literally “the Han River”; in use, “Seoul's shared living room”.

items.sourceNote: Not just geography — infrastructure for joy: picnic blankets, rental tents, 라면 vending machines that cook it for you, and delivery 치킨 that finds your GPS pin on the grass. 한강 가자! proposes an entire genre of evening. The phrase 한강 뷰 (river view) also moves real estate prices by fortunes.

items.english: someone who thinks their small world is the whole world

target.natural_english: someone who thinks their small world is the whole world
target.literal_gap: Literally “a frog inside a well”; in use, “someone who thinks their small world is the whole world”.

items.sourceNote: The classic proverb — the frog believes the circle of sky above its well is all the sky there is. Deployed for provincialism of every kind, including one's own: 저는 우물 안 개구리였어요 is a humble way to say travel changed you. M6's position noun 안 doing literary work.

target.literal_gap: Literally “even Geumgang Mountain, viewing-after-eating”; in use, “food first, everything else second”.

items.sourceNote: The proverb ranks Korea's most legendary mountain BELOW lunch: even the finest scenery is best 식후 — after eating (M13's 후!) — 경 (the viewing of 경치). Quoted before every itinerary is rearranged around a 맛집. The national priorities, notarized in proverb form.

target.literal_gap: Literally “leave home and it's hardship”; in use, “there's no place like home”.

items.sourceNote: 고생 (suffering) begins at your own 현관, says the proverb — beds too hard, food too strange, 짐 too heavy. Said half-jokingly while packing and wholly sincerely while unpacking. Where Dorothy needed ruby slippers, Korean needed one conditional — M20's -면, doing folk wisdom.

items.english: the country, shrunk to three hours

target.natural_english: the country, shrunk to three hours
target.literal_gap: Literally “Korea Train eXpress”; in use, “the country, shrunk to three hours”.

items.sourceNote: Seoul to Busan in under three hours — the bullet train made the whole peninsula a day trip, and 당일치기 (same-day round trip) a lifestyle. Book a window seat on the right side heading south; the 바다 appears just before 부산 and the whole carriage looks up.

target.literal_gap: Literally “it doesn't even become words”; in use, “no way! / that's nonsense”.

items.sourceNote: Fully decodable with owned parts: M4's 말 + M2's 도 + M10's 안 돼요 (here in M19's 반말). A claim so wrong it can't even assemble into speech. The reflex reaction to 소문, 거짓말, and prices in 명동. Polite version: 말도 안 돼요.

target.literal_gap: Literally “it's wrong!”; in use, “(very often) it's just different”.

items.sourceNote: Koreans habitually say 틀리다 (to be wrong — M15) where 다르다 (to be different — M24) belongs: 우리는 성격이 틀려요 means 'our personalities are DIFFERENT,' not wrong. Textbooks scold; speech ignores. Remember the split the other way: 맞고/틀리고 is for answers, 같고/다르고 is for comparisons — and enjoy owning a distinction natives blur.

gloss.gloss: as much as you know, it is seen

target.literal_gap: Literally “as much as you know, it is seen”; in use, “you see what you know”.

items.sourceNote: The saying behind every museum trip (popularized by art historian 유홍준) — built on M24's own machinery: 아는 is 알다 wearing the -는 badge, ㄹ dropped. 만큼 ('as much as') is Ring 2 glue, previewed. Why the 궁 you visited in M23 gets better with every module you finish.

target.literal_gap: Literally “to eat seaweed soup”; in use, “birthday ritual — or exam failure”.

items.sourceNote: Two jobs, one bowl. New mothers eat 미역국 to recover, so every birthday you eat it in tribute to yours. But said after an exam — 미역국 먹었어요 — it means you FAILED: seaweed is slippery, and you slipped right off the pass list. 시험 때 (this module's glue) it is banned from the table; that's how seriously the superstition is taken.

target.literal_gap: Literally “first-birthday grab”; in use, “the baby picks its future”.

items.sourceNote: The centerpiece of the 돌잔치 (M22's 돌 + M25's 잔치 — the note that promised a party delivers). Objects are spread before the one-year-old: 실 (thread) for long life, 돈 for wealth, 연필 for scholarship — modern tables add microphones, stethoscopes, and computer mice. The baby grabs one; destiny is declared; the room cheers; the photo lasts forever.

target.literal_gap: Literally “one hundred days”; in use, “the milestone worth a party”.

items.sourceNote: M9's 백 + M25's 일, self-assembled. Babies get a 백일 celebration — from the era when surviving a hundred days was the hard part — and couples count 백일 anniversaries before switching to years (M19's 커플 culture, timestamped). Korea counts what it treasures, in days.

target.literal_gap: Literally “the beginning is half”; in use, “well begun is half done”.

items.sourceNote: M8's 시작하다's noun + M5's 반 (half) + the plain copula: starting IS half the work. Quoted at every January gym, every first Korean lesson — and at the end of Ring 1, where the math finally flatters you: you started at 안녕하세요, so the rest was the other half.

target.literal_gap: Literally “you suffered”; in use, “good job / well done”.

items.sourceNote: Korean praises the STRUGGLE, not the result — 'you suffered' is the warm thing said after exams, work, and long days, kin to M16's 수고하셨습니다. The 고생 of M23's 집 떠나면 고생이다, now aimed at you kindly. Reply: 아니에요 — or say it back.

gloss.gloss: to drink the kimchi soup first

target.literal_gap: Literally “to drink the kimchi soup first”; in use, “counting your chickens”.

items.sourceNote: The full proverb: someone promises you 떡, and you drink the digestive kimchi-water before the rice cake even arrives. M6's 부터 (starting-from) doing idiom work: celebrating FROM the soup onward, prematurely. Said, smiling, to anyone planning the victory party early.

target.literal_gap: Literally “height is big”; in use, “(someone) is tall”.

items.sourceNote: Korean has no verb for 'to be tall' — height is a possession that is big or small: 키가 커요/작아요. Same chassis as 인기가 많아요 (M17) and 정이 많아요 (M26): pick a noun, measure it, let the subject own it. Asking someone's height: 키가 어떻게 되세요? — the polite how-does-it-become.

target.literal_gap: Literally “east-west-south-north”; in use, “the four directions (in Korean order)”.

items.sourceNote: English says north-south-east-west; Korean says 동서남북 — east first, where the sun rises. The order is fixed like a spell: compass apps, feng-shui talk, and the idiom 동서남북을 모르다 (to not know east from west — to be utterly lost) all run east-first. M27's compass words, in their native sort order.

target.literal_gap: Literally “sleep doesn't come”; in use, “I can't sleep”.

items.sourceNote: You don't fail to sleep in Korean — sleep fails to ARRIVE. Same forecast grammar as 비가 와요 (M11) and 화가 나요 (M19): inner states are weather, and you're just the reporter. Related bulletins: 생각이 안 나요 (the thought won't surface), 이해가 안 돼요 (understanding won't engage).

gloss.gloss: I shall go to school and come back

target.literal_gap: Literally “I shall go to school and come back”; in use, “bye — leaving for school!”.

items.sourceNote: The departure formula every Korean child fires at the front door — M28's round-trip verb wearing M18's -겠- (the 잘 먹겠습니다 machinery). The promise built into the verb is the point: not just going — returning. The parental reply: 다녀와 (M19's 반말, warm edition), or 잘 다녀오세요 going up the ladder.

gloss.gloss: even put in the eye, it wouldn't hurt

target.literal_gap: Literally “even put in the eye, it wouldn't hurt”; in use, “utterly precious (usually a grandchild)”.

items.sourceNote: The maximum-affection idiom: M28's 넣다 putting a beloved somewhere famously intolerant of foreign objects (M14's 눈 + 아프다), and the eye not minding. Grandmothers deploy it about grandchildren; couples about each other in early episodes. Anatomically alarming, emotionally exact.

items.english: pain, sympathy, exhaustion, or delight — context decides

target.natural_english: pain, sympathy, exhaustion, or delight — context decides
target.literal_gap: Literally “(an exhalation)”; in use, “pain, sympathy, exhaustion, or delight — context decides”.

items.sourceNote: The national sigh has four jobs: pain (아이고 허리야 — my back), sympathy (아이고, 어떡해 — oh no, you poor thing), exhaustion (the sound of sitting down after fifty — involuntary, guaranteed), and delight (아이고 예뻐라, at babies). Korean grandparents conduct entire conversations in it. Often clipped to 아이고이고이고 under real duress.

target.literal_gap: Literally “any thing whatsoever”; in use, “whatever's fine (the non-answer)”.

items.sourceNote: M29's 아무 + 거 + -나: the answer to 뭐 먹을까? that decides nothing — and, famously, the answer that means the asker must now read minds (M16's 눈치, activated). Couples cite it in arguments; menus fear it. The positive twin of 아무도 없어요's emptiness.

target.literal_gap: Literally “indeed it is so”; in use, “I know, right?”.

items.sourceNote: The 그렇다 machine's agreement setting: warm, low-effort, endlessly repeatable. 날씨가 덥네요 — 그러게요. Someone states the obvious; you co-sign it; society functions. Casual form 그러게, often doubled (그러게 말이야 — you're TELLING me).

items.english: clear lemon-lime soda — and a satisfying moment

target.natural_english: clear lemon-lime soda — and a satisfying moment
target.literal_gap: Literally “cider”; in use, “clear lemon-lime soda — and a satisfying moment”.

items.sourceNote: The false friend of the beverage aisle: 사이다 is Sprite-style soda, no apples involved. Its slang career is better: a 사이다 moment is one that fizzes away frustration — the sharp comeback, the villain's comeuppance. The opposite is 고구마 (sweet potato): dense, dry, stuck in your throat. Korean reviews grade dramas in soda and root vegetables.

target.literal_gap: Literally “chicken flesh”; in use, “goosebumps — especially at couples' PDA”.

items.sourceNote: M30's 닭 + 살 (flesh): goosebumps, from cold, from horror — and, most productively, from public displays of affection. A 닭살 커플 (M19's 커플) is one whose sweetness raises bumps on bystanders. 닭살 돋아! — I've got goosebumps! — is the standard heckle, deployed with love.

items.english: something you can see but never have

target.natural_english: something you can see but never have
target.literal_gap: Literally “rice cake in a picture”; in use, “something you can see but never have”.

items.sourceNote: M15's 그림 + M18's 떡: the painted rice cake feeds nobody. Deployed at real-estate listings, sports cars, and 딸기 뷔페 reservations that sold out. English pies live in the sky; Korean rice cakes hang in frames — both stay uneaten.

target.literal_gap: Literally “frozen-to-death, still iced”; in use, “an iced-americano loyalist”.

items.sourceNote: 얼어 죽어도 아이스 아메리카노 — 'even if I freeze to death: iced americano' — first-syllabled into a personality type. Korea drinks 아아 through blizzards; the word salutes the commitment. M14's 죽다-hyperbole and Reading 4's shrinker, in one glass.

items.english: tragicomic — funny and sad at once

target.natural_english: tragicomic — funny and sad at once
target.literal_gap: Literally “laugh-sad”; in use, “tragicomic — funny and sad at once”.

items.sourceNote: 웃기다 (M19) welded to 슬프다 (M7): the word for memes that hit too close, comedies about your own life, and 월요일 아침. English needs a sentence; Korean fused two adjectives and moved on. Conjugates like 슬프다: 웃퍼요.

target.literal_gap: Literally “they shorten every-darn-thing”; in use, “slang about slang (meta-준말)”.

items.sourceNote: 별걸 다 줄인다 — 'they abbreviate EVERYTHING' — which is itself an abbreviation: the complaint about first-syllabling, first-syllabled. Deployed by the previous generation at the current one, forever. Reading 4's pressure rule, aware of itself.

items.english: read the room — know when you're wanted

target.natural_english: read the room — know when you're wanted

gloss.gloss: join when joining, leave when leaving

target.literal_gap: Literally “join when joining, leave when leaving”; in use, “read the room — know when you're wanted”.

items.sourceNote: 낄 때 끼고 빠질 때 빠져라, first-syllabled: the social skill of knowing which conversations include you. M16's 눈치 as an imperative — what the 꼰대 lacks and the 인싸 has calibrated to the millimeter.

items.english: the strong and the weak (in any relationship)

target.natural_english: the strong and the weak (in any relationship)
target.literal_gap: Literally “party A and party B”; in use, “the strong and the weak (in any relationship)”.

items.sourceNote: Contract language escaped the contract: 갑 is the stronger party, 을 the weaker — landlord/tenant, brand/franchisee, boss/intern. 갑질 is 갑 abusing the slope; 을의 눈물 (the eul's tears) headlines labor news. Two legal placeholders that became a national vocabulary of power — and yes, that's M30's formal 과 holding them together.

target.literal_gap: Literally “business — middle”; in use, “open / currently in operation”.

items.sourceNote: The ○○ 중 machine: hang 중 (middle, 中) after any noun and it means in-the-middle-of-it — 영업 중 (open), 공사 중 (under construction), 통화 중 (on a call), 회의 중 (in a meeting), 사용 중 (occupied), 다이어트 중 (don't offer cake). One borrowed syllable runs every busy-sign, door hanger, and status message in the country.

items.english: talent belongs where it can thrive — so everyone heads for the capital

target.natural_english: talent belongs where it can thrive — so everyone heads for the capital

gloss.gloss: horses to Jeju, people to Seoul

target.literal_gap: Literally “horses to Jeju, people to Seoul”; in use, “talent belongs where it can thrive — so everyone heads for the capital”.

items.sourceNote: The full proverb: 말은 나면 제주도로 보내고, 사람은 나면 서울로 보내라 — send a foal to Jeju (the horse pastures), send a child to Seoul (the opportunity). Radar inside: this 말 is HORSE, not speech (말씀's humble cousin) — one syllable, two creatures. Centuries old and still the country's operating logic; see 서울 공화국 for what it did to the map.

items.english: everything in Korea concentrates in the capital region

target.natural_english: everything in Korea concentrates in the capital region
target.literal_gap: Literally “the Republic of Seoul”; in use, “everything in Korea concentrates in the capital region”.

items.sourceNote: Half the population lives in 서울 + 경기도 + 인천; the jobs, universities, hospitals, and broadcasters crowd in with them. 공화국 = republic (공화 + your country-국) — the phrase Koreans reach for when complaining that the other eight 도 might as well be scenery. The horse proverb is how it started; the KTX (M23) is how it accelerated.

items.english: all of Korea — everywhere in the country

target.natural_english: all of Korea — everywhere in the country
target.literal_gap: Literally “eight provinces”; in use, “all of Korea — everywhere in the country”.

items.sourceNote: Joseon carved the country into eight 도 in 1413 — 경기, 강원, 충청, 전라, 경상, plus three now north of the border (평안, 함경, 황해). The count stuck as an idiom for 'the whole country' centuries after the map moved on: 팔도 사투리 (dialects from everywhere), 전국 팔도, and the 팔도 instant-noodle brand in every convenience store. M14's 팔 + this module's 도 — two syllables, six hundred years of map.

items.english: sorry, what did you say? (or, with heat: WHAT?!)

target.natural_english: sorry, what did you say? (or, with heat: WHAT?!)
target.literal_gap: Literally “you say — what?”; in use, “sorry, what did you say? (or, with heat: WHAT?!)”.

items.sourceNote: The quote-machine as a reflex: 뭐라고 (해요) with the reporting verb dropped entirely. Flat intonation = 'come again?'; rising heat = the last thing said was outrageous. Among friends it's 뭐라고? — and in texts it shrinks further to 머라고/뭐라구. One quoting particle, the whole spectrum from hard-of-hearing to how-dare-you.

items.english: I hear they're coming — hearsay in one syllable

target.natural_english: I hear they're coming — hearsay in one syllable
target.literal_gap: Literally “come — (says, shrunk)”; in use, “I hear they're coming — hearsay in one syllable”.

items.sourceNote: -다고 해요 compressed to -대요 (and -라고 해요 to -래요) — the 준말 reading's frequency-pressure law applied to grammar itself. 온다고 해요 → 온대요; 학생이라고 해요 → 학생이래요. This is gossip's native gear: 결혼한대요! (I hear they're getting married!). Recognize it now; Ring 2 will have you producing it soon enough.

items.english: a star the whole country has adopted

target.natural_english: a star the whole country has adopted
target.literal_gap: Literally “the nation's little sister”; in use, “a star the whole country has adopted”.

items.sourceNote: 국민 as a prefix nationalizes affection: 국민 여동생 (여자 + M4's 동생 — the beloved young star everyone claims as family), 국민 MC (the host in every living room), 국민 간식 (the national snack — 떡볶이 holds the title). When fifty million people agree on something, Korean files it under the family register — 우리나라 logic (M27), one shelf over.

items.english: please take care of me — the first-meeting formula

target.natural_english: please take care of me — the first-meeting formula
target.literal_gap: Literally “I entrust (it/myself) to you well”; in use, “please take care of me — the first-meeting formula”.

items.sourceNote: Said when joining a team, meeting in-laws, starting lessons — anywhere a relationship begins. English has no slot for it: you're formally handing yourself over and trusting the other side to be kind. Built from owned parts: M10's 잘 + this module's 부탁 + M9's humble 드리다 in M4's 합니다체. Answer it with a smile and the same phrase back.

gloss.gloss: ah is one thing, eo is another

target.literal_gap: Literally “ah is one thing, eo is another”; in use, “HOW you say it changes everything”.

items.sourceNote: A 속담 about speech itself, built from two Module-1 vowels: swap ㅏ for ㅓ and the word changes — 맛 becomes 멋 (taste becomes style, M3/M21), 살 becomes 설. So mind your delivery: the same message lands warm or cold depending on the syllable you pick. The proverb your confusables drill has been acting out since day one. Deploy it when someone says the right thing the wrong way.

target.literal_gap: Literally “empty words”; in use, “polite formulas nobody means literally”.

items.sourceNote: 언제 밥 한번 먹어요! (let's grab a meal sometime!) usually isn't an invitation — it's a warm goodbye. 놀러 오세요! doesn't always mean come over. 빈말 (비다 empty + 말 speech) is the lubricant register: kindness performed, not promised. The test: a real invitation comes with a date (M25's machine). Don't be hurt when the meal never happens — and learn to make the noises back.

items.english: frazzled — too swamped to think straight

target.natural_english: frazzled — too swamped to think straight
target.literal_gap: Literally “there is no mind/spirit”; in use, “frazzled — too swamped to think straight”.

items.sourceNote: The national state of being: mornings, Mondays, moving day, parenthood — all 정신이 없어요. It doubles as an apology-adjacent greeting (요즘 정신이 없어서 연락 못 했어요 = sorry, life ate me) and the adverb 정신없이 means 'in a blur': 정신없이 바빴어요. The 있다-factory's spookiest product — Korean measures sanity in stock levels.

target.literal_gap: Literally “Monday sickness”; in use, “the Monday blues, diagnosed”.

items.sourceNote: 월요일 (M5's Moon-day) + 병 (M14's illness): the Monday blues, but Korean files it as a medical condition — and everyone claims the diagnosis. 월요병 때문에 우울해요 is a complete, socially valid excuse. The -병 suffix productively diagnoses anything: 공주병 (princess sickness — vanity), 게으름병 (chronic laziness). The five-day workweek's most honest word.

target.literal_gap: Literally “don't even dream the dream”; in use, “don't even THINK about it”.

items.sourceNote: Fully decodable ambition-crushing: M8's 꿈 + M2's 도 (even) + dream-verb 꾸다 + M19's bare -지 마. Korean dreams are 'dreamed' with their own verb (꿈을 꾸다 — cognate object, like singing a song: 노래를 부르다), so forbidding the dream forbids the wanting. Deploy on friends eyeing your last piece of 치킨.

gloss.gloss: a three-year-old's habit goes until eighty

target.literal_gap: Literally “a three-year-old's habit goes until eighty”; in use, “old habits die hard — so raise them well from the start”.

items.sourceNote: Nearly every word is yours: M5's 세 살, this module's 버릇, M30's 여든, M6's 까지, and 가다 in the plain form the quote-machine taught you to read. Korea's most-quoted parenting proverb — deployed on nail-biters, phone-checkers, and anyone whose 버릇 outlived its excuse. The pedagogy checks out: this module is literally about what sticks.

items.english: to fall in love — same accident, same grammar

target.natural_english: to fall in love — same accident, same grammar
target.literal_gap: Literally “to fall into love”; in use, “to fall in love — same accident, same grammar”.

items.sourceNote: Korean and English independently agreed: love is a hole you fall into (빠지다 — the same verb as falling into water). No one 사랑에 걸어 들어가다 (walks in); the grammar insists it's an accident. The verb's other jobs sharpen the joke — 드라마에 빠지다, 게임에 빠지다: obsession is just love with worse posture.

items.english: greatness can come from humble beginnings

target.natural_english: greatness can come from humble beginnings

gloss.gloss: a dragon rises from a ditch

target.literal_gap: Literally “a dragon rises from a ditch”; in use, “greatness can come from humble beginnings”.

items.sourceNote: 용 = dragon, 개천 = a roadside stream: the classic rags-to-riches proverb, powered by M28's 나다 (the eruption verb — dragons ERUPT from ditches; the grammar knew). Modern Korea argues about whether it's still true — 'the ditch-dragon era is over' is a whole newspaper genre (M32 gave you the vocabulary for that debate). Either way: when a night-shift kid passes the bar exam, this is the headline.

items.english: what a relief — I can stop worrying now

target.natural_english: what a relief — I can stop worrying now
target.literal_gap: Literally “the heart gets set down”; in use, “what a relief — I can stop worrying now”.

items.sourceNote: Korean worry is a carried object: you hold your 마음 (M19) tight until the news is good, then 놓이다 — this module's passive — sets it down for you. Said after the call comes, the test results post, the kid texts back. The active version exists too: 마음을 놓다 = let yourself relax. English exhales; Korean puts the heart down. Same relief, better physics.

gloss.gloss: I got hit by the wind

target.literal_gap: Literally “I got hit by the wind”; in use, “I got stood up”.

items.sourceNote: You dressed up, you waited, they never came — you stood in the wind and the wind is all that showed. M11's 바람 + 맞다 (to be hit — the homograph of M15's 맞다 'correct': one syllable, right answers and rainstorms). The doer's side exists too: 바람맞히다 = to stand someone up. Related but worse: 바람(을) 피우다 = to cheat — in Korean, wind is never good news for couples.

items.english: the silver lining — it could have been so much worse

target.natural_english: the silver lining — it could have been so much worse
target.literal_gap: Literally “good fortune amid misfortune”; in use, “the silver lining — it could have been so much worse”.

items.sourceNote: The phrase Korea reaches for after every fender-bender: 불행 (불- the un- prefix + 행복's happy-행 = misfortune) + S2's 중 (amid) + this module's 다행. 다리를 다쳤지만 불행 중 다행이에요 — broke a leg, but it wasn't the neck. The 불- prefix is a machine of its own (불가능 impossible, 불편 uncomfortable — M12's 편하다 negated); file it, Ring 2 keeps paying it.

items.english: to let go of expectations — want nothing, hurt less

target.natural_english: to let go of expectations — want nothing, hurt less
target.literal_gap: Literally “to empty the heart/mind”; in use, “to let go of expectations — want nothing, hurt less”.

items.sourceNote: Korea's standing prescription for disappointment: before exam results, after breakups, during job hunts — 마음을 비웠어요 means you've released the wanting. Temple-stay Buddhism runs through it (the monks mean it literally), but so does test-day pragmatism: expect nothing, and the result can only surprise you upward. M19's 마음 + this module's 비우다: the heart as a container you can, with practice, pour out.

target.literal_gap: Literally “save the person!”; in use, “HELP! — the emergency scream”.

items.sourceNote: Not 도와주세요 (that's for directions and heavy boxes) — real danger screams 사람 살려!: make-the-person-LIVE, this module's 살리다 in the imperative, particles abandoned because emergencies don't gate. Also deployed in mock horror: buried under work, tickled by friends, facing a spider. The causative party's loudest member; may you only ever use it for the spider.

items.english: high-maintenance — it takes a lot of care

target.natural_english: high-maintenance — it takes a lot of care
target.literal_gap: Literally “many hands go (into it)”; in use, “high-maintenance — it takes a lot of care”.

items.sourceNote: Fully decodable: M8's 손 + M17's 많이 + 가다 — your hands GO to the thing, repeatedly. Said of fiddly recipes (잡채 is the canonical example), needy pets, delicate plants, and — fondly — certain people: 손이 많이 가는 스타일. The caretaking module's own summary: everything in it, from 아기 to 화분, is something 손이 많이 가는. Affection, measured in trips.

items.english: overnight — all at once, out of nowhere

target.natural_english: overnight — all at once, out of nowhere
target.literal_gap: Literally “in one morning”; in use, “overnight — all at once, out of nowhere”.

items.sourceNote: M8's 하루 + M2's 아침 + 에: change compressed into a single morning — 하루아침에 유명해졌어요 (famous overnight — M35's machine at full speed), 하루아침에 바뀌지 않아요 (it won't change overnight — every coach's caveat). Korean picked morning, English picked night; both agree real change usually takes longer than either.

items.english: utterly swamped — not a second to breathe

target.natural_english: utterly swamped — not a second to breathe

gloss.gloss: no gap to open eyes and nose

target.literal_gap: Literally “no gap to open eyes and nose”; in use, “utterly swamped — not a second to breathe”.

items.sourceNote: M14's 눈 and 코 + this module's 뜨다 + 새 — and that 새 is the worn-down 사이 (gap, M6) you just met inside 요새 and 어느새: too busy to open your eyes, let alone the nose (how one opens a nose is not addressed; that's how busy). 눈코 뜰 새 없이 바빴어요 = the week, summarized. The 있다-factory's most breathless product.

items.english: the old custom of running fashionably late

target.natural_english: the old custom of running fashionably late
target.literal_gap: Literally “Korean Time”; in use, “the old custom of running fashionably late”.

items.sourceNote: Konglish, self-deprecating: mid-century Korea joked that appointments ran on 코리안 타임 — 30 minutes behind, no apology needed. The 빨리빨리 era (M8's gap deck) killed it dead: today's Korea is punctual to the minute, and KTX doors forgive nothing. The phrase survives as a tease for late friends — 또 코리안 타임이야? Deploy gently; receive it never (M33's 미리 연락 exists for a reason).
